title: Aldinger v. Howard
lead: An employee tried to litigate her dismissal against county officials and the county in one federal suit, but the county presented a separate statutory jurisdiction problem.

actors.name: Howard
actors.role: County treasurer who allegedly dismissed her

actors.name: Spokane County
actors.role: Proposed defendant on the related state claim

proceedings: District court dismissed Spokane County and entered Rule 54(b) judgment.
Supreme Court affirmed the county dismissal, 6–3.
limits: The discharge account consists of pleading allegations. The decision used the municipal § 1983 exclusion then controlling, later changed by Monell. It did not decide a direct Fourteenth Amendment claim under § 1331, the merits, or every form of pendent-party jurisdiction.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A clerical appointment ends
sections.cue: The employee asks for a hearing
paragraphs: According to Aldinger’s complaint, county treasurer Howard hired her for clerical work in 1971 and, two months later, told her that her performance was excellent but she would be discharged because she was allegedly living with her boyfriend. Howard relied on a Washington law permitting the appointing officer to revoke appointments at pleasure. Aldinger requested a hearing and alleged that none occurred before or after her dismissal.

She sought an injunction against the discharge and compensation for lost salary. Her second amended complaint named Howard, his wife, county commissioners, and Spokane County. Against the officials she invoked 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and the First, Ninth, and Fourteenth Amendments, including procedural due process. Her state-law claim against the county depended on Washington provisions waiving immunity and imposing vicarious liability for officials’ tortious conduct. Everyone was a Washington citizen, so diversity jurisdiction could not bring that claim into federal court.

sections.title: The county leaves the federal action
paragraphs: Under the Supreme Court’s then-controlling interpretation of § 1983, a county was not a covered person. The district court concluded that it therefore lacked power to hear the related state claim against Spokane County. It entered a Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 54(b) judgment allowing an immediate appeal. The Ninth Circuit affirmed under its approach rejecting pendent-party jurisdiction.

The district court had not alternatively decided that it would decline an available jurisdiction as a matter of discretion. The Supreme Court consequently faced a question of statutory power. Although the complaint also mentioned § 1331 and its then-required jurisdictional amount, Aldinger had pursued the county through § 1983, § 1343(3), and pendent jurisdiction. A possible direct Fourteenth Amendment claim under § 1331 had not been resolved below or presented in the certiorari petition, and the Court left it undecided.

sections.title: Related facts do not supply statutory authority
paragraphs: Aldinger relied on United Mine Workers v. Gibbs: the same discharge supplied a common nucleus of operative fact for the federal and state claims, and one proceeding would save resources. She also invoked ancillary jurisdiction and the Federal Rules’ preference for combining related claims and parties.

Justice Rehnquist distinguished Gibbs’s related claims against a defendant already properly before the court from adding another defendant solely on a state claim. Earlier ancillary cases, including disputes over property or funds controlled by a federal court, showed that additional parties sometimes could enter without independent jurisdiction. Those settings could involve claimants otherwise deprived of an effective forum or a judgment that could not work without them. They did not establish an unlimited power whenever claims overlapped. Article III’s permissible reach and trial convenience could not replace Congress’s authorization.

The majority read § 1343(3), the relevant jurisdictional grant, together with § 1983. Because the latter then excluded counties from federal liability, the Court inferred that Congress had also implicitly withheld this means of adding the county on state law. Jurisdiction required both constitutional permission and the absence of an express or implied statutory prohibition.

That was a holding about this statutory combination and party alignment. It did not eliminate independent diversity jurisdiction over municipal corporations or declare all pendent-party jurisdiction unconstitutional. The Court observed that exclusive federal jurisdiction over a claim against the United States might strengthen the argument for hearing related claims together, because only the federal forum could accommodate all of them. It reserved that different problem rather than deciding a Federal Tort Claims Act joinder case.

sections.title: Brennan challenges the inferred prohibition
paragraphs: Justice Brennan, joined by Justices Marshall and Blackmun, would have extended Gibbs to related parties. Added defendants could complicate litigation or raise fairness concerns, but those considerations should inform discretion after jurisdiction exists. Splitting the same facts between state and federal courts wasted resources and could deter civil-rights plaintiffs from using the independent federal forum Congress intended.

Brennan agreed that Congress could prohibit this jurisdiction but found no such prohibition. Exemption from a federally created municipal obligation did not necessarily bar a federal court from enforcing an obligation state law already imposed. His legislative-history analysis distinguished those subjects; the majority read the same historical statements more narrowly as recognition of established diversity jurisdiction.

On June 24, 1976, the Supreme Court affirmed the Ninth Circuit, leaving Spokane County dismissed without deciding whether the discharge violated either federal or state law. In 1978, Monell held that municipalities are § 1983 persons, while rejecting liability based solely on employing a tortfeasor. That later development changed Aldinger’s substantive premise; Aldinger’s 1976 analysis cannot simply be restated as current municipal or supplemental-jurisdiction law.

sources.pinpoint: 427 U.S. at 19–37; Monell, 436 U.S. 658, Part II, as discussed in the reviewed brief
